\chapter{Conmigo, Contigo --- The Word That Says With Twice}
\label{ch:conmigo}
\hlchaptermodality{247}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say with me and with you.}

I can say with me and with you.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[conmigo · contigo]{conmigo · contigo — the word that says \textquotedblleft{}with\textquotedblright{} twice}

\label{lesson:ES-C64-conmigo}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Para mí}, \emph{para ti}. The pattern is steady: preposition, then the stressed pronoun.

One preposition refuses to follow it.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{\textbf{Con}} means \emph{with}. But \emph{with me} is not \emph{con mí}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Vienes} \emph{\textbf{conmigo}}\emph{?} — Are you coming with me?
\end{quote}

Here is where it came from, and it is one of the best stories in the language. Latin did not put \emph{cum} in front of a pronoun; it stuck it on the \textbf{end}: \emph{\textbf{mecum}}, literally \emph{me-with}.

Spanish inherited that as \emph{-migo} — and by then nobody could hear a preposition in it any more. It had become a meaningless tail. So Spanish put \emph{con} back on the \textbf{front}, where prepositions belong.

Which means \emph{\textbf{conmigo}} contains \emph{with} \textbf{twice}: once at each end, in two different languages, fifteen centuries apart. And \emph{contigo} does exactly the same.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
This is the same instinct you saw turn \emph{mucho} into \emph{muy} and \emph{a el} into \emph{al}, running the other way. Spanish reshapes small words to keep them audible — usually by wearing them down, and here, once, by \textbf{doubling} one that had worn away to nothing.

There are only two of these. From \emph{él} onward the ordinary pattern returns: \emph{con él}, \emph{con ella}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{conmigo}, \emph{contigo}, then \emph{con él}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \emph{conmigo} begin with \emph{con} when it already ends in one? (Because the \textbf{old one stopped being audible}.)

How many pronouns do this? (\textbf{Two} — \emph{conmigo}, \emph{contigo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
